title: PLA Posts 6 Sorties May 17 — 4 Enter SW/Eastern ADIZ; 5 PLAN Vessels; 14 Days to HIMARS Deadline; Post-Summit Moderate Pressure Maintained
detail: Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense detected 6 PLA aircraft sorties and 5 PLAN vessels plus 1 official ship operating around Taiwan as of 06:00 local time on May 17, 2026. Of the 6 sorties, 4 entered Taiwan's southwestern and eastern Air Defense Identification Zones — consistent with the PLA's established ADIZ corridor pattern. This represents a moderate-tempo continuation of post-summit PLA activity: sharply below the summit-conclusion day peak of 15 total aircraft (May 15), but above the summit-window lows of 2-3 sorties seen on May 13-14. PLAN naval presence increased slightly to 5 vessels plus 1 official ship, from May 15's 4 PLAN vessels. The full May 2026 sortie sequence now reads: 4 (May 1) → 29 record (May 2) → 1 (May 3) → 2 (May 4) → 1 (May 5) → 0 (May 6) → 22 (May 7) → 12 (May 8) → 8 (May 9) → 12 (May 10) → 7 (May 11) → 9 (May 12) → 2 (May 13) → 3 (May 14) → 15 (May 15) → 6 (May 17). AEI's May 15 China & Taiwan Update reported 169 ADIZ incursions in April 2026 total — significantly lower than the same period in 2025, following the Justice Mission-2025 December drills. The PRC research vessel Tongji, which conducted undersea research in waters surrounding Taiwan May 7-11, has returned to the PRC. The HIMARS payment deadline is now 14 days away (May 31). ROC Armed Forces monitored the incursions and deployed CAP aircraft, naval vessels, and coastal missile systems in response.

title: Post-Trump-Xi Summit Assessments: CFR — 'Decent Peace But Taiwan Tests Begin'; Seoul Economic Daily — 'Conflicting Claims on Taiwan'; Atlantic Council — Summit 'Underwhelming' on Taiwan
detail: By May 17, 2026, leading international policy institutions had published their post-Trump-Xi summit assessments, uniformly identifying Taiwan as the central unresolved issue. The Council on Foreign Relations headlined its analysis 'Beyond Taiwan, a Decent Peace at the Trump-Xi Summit' — acknowledging the summit produced general diplomatic calm but identifying Taiwan's security tests as the defining near-term challenge, beginning with the $14B arms package decision and HIMARS deadline. The Atlantic Council's dispatch was more pointed: 'Where's the Beef? Trump's Underwhelming Meeting with Xi' — noting that on Taiwan, Trump delivered Xi substantial concessions (arms 'in abeyance,' Taiwan told to 'cool it') while receiving little in return. Seoul Economic Daily (May 17) headlined: 'Trump-Xi Summit Ends With Conflicting Claims on Tariffs, Taiwan' — the divergent US and PRC narratives producing different takeaways for Taiwan security watchers. The consensus among analysts: the summit was diplomatically stabilizing for US-China relations broadly but produced no binding commitments on Taiwan, Trump's 'negotiating chip' framing introduced unprecedented transactionalism into Taiwan's security equation, and the Taiwan tests that Bloomberg predicted ('Taiwan will test ties soon') have effectively already begun with Trump's post-summit arms clarification. Japan-Philippines defense coordination (Japanese Defense Minister Koizumi met Philippine counterpart Teodoro on May 5) continues to develop the regional Taiwan contingency coalition structure, providing some institutional continuity beneath the summit ambiguity.
